draft.title: Associations between categorical variables
card: A two-way table shows counts for two categorical variables at once. One variable runs down the rows and the other across the columns.

Raw counts can mislead when the groups differ in size. So turn the counts into percentages of each column total, or each row total, using the variable that sorts people into the groups being compared.
Percentages are taken within each group being compared. Then compare them across the groups. Example: 30 of 60 Year 11 students walk to school (50%), and 20 of 80 Year 12 students do (25%).

If the percentages differ clearly between the groups, the variables may be related. This is called an association. If they are about the same, there is no association. In the example, walking may be associated with year level.
draft.remember: Find percentages within each group being compared, then compare them. Clearly different percentages mean the variables may be related.

a.q: In a survey, 24 of 48 Year 7 students and 50 of 100 Year 8 students chose pizza as their favourite food. What does this show about year level and food choice?
opts: No association, as 50% of each year level chose pizza
An association, as Year 8 has 26 more students who chose it
An association, as 32% of those who chose it are in Year 7
An association, as the counts 24 and 50 clearly differ
a.why: Year 7: 24 ÷ 48 = 50%. Year 8: 50 ÷ 100 = 50%. The percentages within each year level are the same, so there is no association. The counts differ only because the year levels differ in size.
a.clue: Turn each count into a percentage of its own year level.

b.q: In a survey, 42 of 60 students in Town A and 30 of 120 students in Town B use public transport to get to school. Which statement is correct?
opts: Use may be related to town, 70% to 25%
Use may be related to town, 42% to 30%
Use is not related to town, as 42 is more than 30
Use is not related to town, as 40% of all students use it
b.why: Town A: 42 ÷ 60 = 70%. Town B: 30 ÷ 120 = 25%. The percentages differ clearly, so the variables may be related. The numbers 42 and 30 are counts, not percentages.
b.clue: Divide each count by its own town total, not the overall total.

a.best: No association, as 50% of each year level chose pizza

b.best: Use may be related to town, 70% to 25%
